speechtext:
that Bill C-241, an Act to provide assistance for victims of crime, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in specific terms 1 am asking the House of Commons to give second reading to Bill C-241 which enacts the Crime Victims Assistance Act. My real purpose is to present the broader context of the subject of victims of crime. The role of victims in the criminal process has never been recognized in Canada and my purpose is to draw attention to that fact.
Hopefully the House and the committees of the House will give consideration in the future to the role of victims of crime in the criminal process. It goes without saying, Mr. Speaker, that I would accept an amendment to the motion to give second reading that would allow the subject matter of the

January 23, 1986
Crime Victims Assistance Act
status of victims of crime to be referred to an appropriate committee of the House such as the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
I will begin by explaining my motive in presenting this Bill to the House of Commons. Over many years of involvement with the administration of justice in Canada, I have noted on numerous occasions that victims of crime have in fact been the victims of the court process as well as victims of the criminal act which resulted in the court process. In many cases victims of crime are unaware of the criminal proceedings and the investigations leading up to the actual case before the court in Canada and, generally speaking, have no information on the investigation or the court processes. That is a matter to which I attempted to direct attention in the Bill.
Apart from that, Mr. Speaker, time and again we have seen persons victimized by criminal acts going without compensation. That is a very difficult subject involving both federal and provincial jurisdictions. Steps have been taken in many provinces and by the Government of Canada to provide a method of compensation. However, it is always difficult for the victim of a crime, arid the family of a victim of a crime, to see a criminal offender walk away from a court after having inflicted personal injury or committed damage to property of the victim of a crime, without any requirement that any compensation be made or any retribution be given by the perpetrator of the crime. That is the second point that is addressed in this Bill.
I would also like to make a few remarks generally about Private Members' Bills. I know that as solicitors in the Department of Justice review a Bill such as this there will be a tendency to pick away, not only at the letter of the law, but at the substance of it, and engage in constitutional and jurisdictional arguments. It is not the duty of a private Member who presents a Bill in the House of Commons to dot all the "i"s, and cross all the "t"s and come up with a perfect piece of legislation. A private Member's Bill is really a vehicle for focussing attention on the subject matter of the Bill. I hope that if and when lawyers in the Department of Justice and elsewhere in the Government service have an opportunity to review the provisions of the Bill they will realize that the general intention is to aid and assist victims of crime rather than to establish a legal precedent that will stand the test of time, one that is emblazoned in iron or chiselled in stone. It is simply a document that presents a possible beginning to the resolution of a real social problem. It is with that in mind, Mr. Speaker, that I take the liberty of pointing out to the House of Commons some of the provisions of this Bill.
Basically, this legislation dealing with assistance to victims of crime has two major features. First, it makes provision for informing the victim of a crime, or the family of a victim in the case of a fatality, of the facts concerning the investigation as the investigation by the police and other officers proceeds. When that investigation reaches the point of court action, which, as my legal colleagues know, under a criminal process
begins with the laying of an information against an accused person, the victim then is informed of the fact and of all the subsequent proceedings in respect of that information.
I am sure many lawyers may quarrel with the process and procedures that have been suggested by this Bill, but the fact is that in our criminal process under the Criminal Code of Canada an informant or person who lays an information-the person who actually makes the charge-has a status in the legal proceedings. Therefore, if the victim of a crime is also the informant, in that capacity they have a right to receive information and documentation concerning the case before the courts.
I am simply giving to any and all victims of a crime, or representatives of the victim of a crime in the case of a fatality, the status of informant and the right on their part and the obligation on the part of the police and the court officials to keep that victim or victim's representative informed of all the proceedings. I do not believe there is anything novel or difficult about that concept.
The second major feature of the Bill concerns a right given to a victim or the family, in the case of a deceased victim, to recover compensation from the offender. Those provisions may present greater difficulty. Let me explain my motive in attempting to codify this right into law.
Based on my experience, in many cases unless the compensation that might be provided to a victim of crime is provided quickly and expeditiously, with a minimum of legal difficulty, no compensation whatever will be recovered. It is trite to say that the victim of a crime has a right to sue in civil courts, a right that is protected by many provisions, both for the plaintiff, or claimant, and the defendant, or the person defending against the claim. However, there is a need and I believe a right on the part of a victim of crime in our society to more immediate redress.
I have attempted to establish that process and procedure which would provide that more immediate redress. I direct Members attention to that specific provision of the bill. Again, it is not without fault or difficulty and I would be the last to pretend that it does not present certain difficulties. However, it is based on a known and recognized principle of criminal law. For many years the Criminal Code of Canada has provided for restitution as part of the punishment or penalty imposed on the accused and convicted person. It is not entirely novel although it may be a new approach.
The point of the Bill is to provide two major features to aid and assist a victim of a crime. The first feature is that the victim receives information from the police and other officials with respect to the investigation of the crime and that they are kept informed of the court proceedings after a charge is laid and a court process is begun.
The second feature is a right to quick redress and compensation in certain circumstances and cases. I do not expect the House of Commons to endorse this Bill and all its provisions. However, I believe there is a real interest not only in the House but across the country to provide some assistance to
January 23, 1986

victims of crime. If that is the desire of the House, and I believe it is the desire of Canadians, I ask the House to take some action to see that this subject matter is continued and attention is focused on it through our parliamentary process.
Dealing more generally with the subject of victims of crime, I want to point out to Members, as it has been pointed out to me on many occasions, that victims of crime have no role in the criminal justice system. They are the forgotten people. Over the years we have seen a great deal of public attention focused on the rights of persons suspected of criminal offences and the rights of persons charged with criminal offences. However, very little attention has been focused on the victims of criminal acts. I believe it is time that we change this and do something about the victims of crime.
I was pleased to be one of the Members of the House to have endorsed the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and all of its provisions that are applicable to persons who are suspected and charged with crime. I think we have some obligation to look at the other side of the coin. I cannot believe that Members of the House do not agree with that proposition.
I want to bring two specific points to the attention of Members of the House. One is the cost of the crime in relation to the victims of crime. I have a report that emanated from the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Beatty) that gives some details of the cost of crime to victims in Canada. I will simply provide one statistic contained in that report. As a result of a survey conducted through seven cities in Canada, it was determined that the cost of crime to victims in those seven cities in a one-year period was $431 million. That amount is made up of $211 million in unrecovered property and cash; $41.9 million in damage to property; $7 million in associated medical expenses and lost wages and, apart from that direct loss, claims of $170 million were paid out to victims by insurance companies. Therefore, we are talking about a significant problem and one that affects many Canadians.
In a more ideal society than we have in Canada in 1986-I know we are working to make it a better society-we would have a victim's bill of rights. I am sure many agree that victims of crime need special protection and ought to have special consideration under the law. A victim's bill of rights has been established, as I understand it, in 30 state legislature across the United States.
One might ask: What is a victim's bill of rights? I understand that it is a reference to a package of concerns to establish fair standards for treatment of victims and witnesses. While the legislation apparently varies from state to state, these standards include protection from intimidation and harm, the right to information about the case, the right to submit a statement to the court at the time of sentencing during plea bargaining or case dismissal, the return of property and the right to lost employment or wages.
I have only addressed two elements of a victim's bill of rights in Bill C-241. They are the right to information and a method of providing immediate redress and compensation. We still have a long way to go. It is not in any way a perfect document, and I am sure my colleagues in the House will
Crime Victims Assistance Act
remind me of that very soon. However, it is simply a start. I am attempting to draw attention to the plight of victims of crime. I am trying to demonstrate that something can be done through legislation to redress some of the wrongs of the past.
I am simply asking the House to make a start by referring the subject matter of this Bill to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I hope my colleagues in the House will see fit to take that action so we may look at the neglected people in the criminal justice system, the victims of crime.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise on this important legislation to indicate on behalf of the New Democratic Party, as Justice spokesman for my Party, that we fully support the reference of the subject matter to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
Certainly the question of victims' rights and the extent to which victims have been ignored traditionally in the criminal justice process is one which has, over the last three or four years, been very much coming to the fore. There have been a number of conferences, books and draft conventions. Indeed, the United Nations dealt with the subject at the last congress on the prevention of crime.
The whole question of the status of victims of crime has been drawn to my attention, not just in an abstract way but in a very real way, through a number of families, including a family in my own constituency of Burnaby, a mother, Mrs. Jacqueline Helm, whose daughter was murdered and who came to my office afterward and told me about the way in which her family was denied access to information and were

January 23, 1986
Crime Victims Assistance Act
systematically dealt with in a manner that was insensitive and which failed to reflect the concerns they had about the outcome of the trial, their sense of loss, and their lack of awareness of what was going on.
There are a couple of major concerns in the area of victims' rights. It is the view of victims of crime, and I am referring now to the report of the Canadian Federal Provincial Task Force on Justice for Victims of Crime, that they need more assistance to deal with their losses and suffering.
In speaking of the families of victims the task force stated that in addition they believe they should be compensated adequately for any loss or suffering which they have endured. Many of them also feel that they need to be active participants in the justice process. Most important, I hear the cry for more information and awareness about what is going on.
Many victims find themselves confused and bewildered by the criminal justice system, not just in terms of the specific case but basic questions as to how the system operates. Why is it the property they may have had stolen from them cannot be returned to them immediately? Why was a particular charge reduced? What was the nature of the plea bargaining that took place? Why did the trial have to be adjourned? Why was the individual not informed as a victim when the jury were to come in with their verdict? Why was restitution not ordered? What sort of criminal injuries compensation is available? And so on.
I see the Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) is in the House today. I want to commend the work he has done on behalf of victims of crime. Since he was first elected as a Member he has worked particularly hard with a group "Victims and Violence" and Don Sullivan to try to improve the quality of services to victims in Canada.
There is not just a need for information, Mr. Speaker, but as well the need for services for victims. I would point out the acute shortage of transition houses and rape crisis centres in our communities for victims of sexual assault, the importance of funding for crisis intervention centres and the training of workers within the system to recognize and respond to the needs of victims and to help the victims financially where there has been loss and suffering.
I think it is also important that we as a Parliament do what we can to prevent crime and thus to reduce the number of victims and potential victims of crime. We must attack the causes of crime.
The Senate committee has identified a number of causes in an excellent report which that Committee called "Child at Risk". The Canadian Council on Social Development and the Canadian Criminal Justice Association have talked about the importance of crime prevention through social development programs; attacking unemployment, particularly among young people; attacking poverty and the appallingly inadequate levels of welfare, particularly for single parents; the enhancing of programs for dealing with learning disabilities; the whole question of violence in our society, violence on TV, for example, and in the media; reducing the level of violence, the
Rambo mentality which is so prevalent and the video games which children are playing involving killing as many potential victims as possible within as short a time as possible. We have to look at the violence ethic in our society. We have to look at effective forms of gun control to ensure that the level of violence is reduced and the number of potential victims is reduced.
We must not forget that there are also victims of crime within the prison system. Because people lose their liberty and are sentenced to terms of imprisonment does not mean they lose all of their rights. We must ensure where prisoners are victims of violence, as at Archambault prison not that long ago, that they too are provided with services. Hopefully that kind of violence at the hands of the state will not be tolerated or permitted.
As well, it is important we not just consider traditional forms of crime and traditional victims. One of the important themes of the United Nations in the work it has done on victims of crime is to ensure consideration of non traditional forms of crime as well. We must consider the victims of environmental pollution; victims of the destruction of our environment and our native people who are the victims of mercury poisoning in northwestern Ontario. We have to look at victims of environmental crime. Working men and women who are maimed and killed on the job are victims, and victims of what I consider to be crimes. We must look at abuses of power in our society, at corporate fraud, at negligence in the pursuit of profit and the unsafe and hazardous products that are inflicted upon us. There are victims in those areas of crime as well.
The range of concerns which must be addressed by the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs in examining the whole question of victims' rights is very broad indeed. We must look at victim input in the whole question of the laying of charges, victims' rights to fundamental information, pre-trial hearings, perhaps involving the victim and the accused and what is the onus of the burden of proof. As well we must look at the whole question of victim impact statements. This issue has been raised, and the implications have to be carefully examined. We have the role of the victim in the sentencing process and methods of determining compensation for victims. The Justice Committee will have an onerous task ahead of it.
1 commend the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) for bringing this matter before the House. Certainly while I do have some questions about the specific details of his private Members' Bill, 1 am pleased to rise in support of the reference of this important subject matter for the rights of victims of crime and their families to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I hope that that committee will give this subject the full and comprehensive study it so deserves.

Mr. Speaker, the debate over the last few moments indicates very clearly
January 23, 1986

that we now have before the House an idea whose time has come. I salute the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) for bringing the matter of compensation for victims of crime to the attention of the thirty-third Parliament. As clearly evidenced by what was said by the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) and the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), this matter will have the support of Hon. Members on all sides of the House to go to committee where it can be thoroughly aired and proper legislation brought forward.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby, in his usual scholarly way, referred to the many studies and works which have gone on up until now to deal with aspects of this problem. The Hon. Member for Halifax West clearly outlined why this is timely. Certainly in the evolution of law, legal recourse and remedy in the country, it has been an important development in shifting from tort law to a statutory right for compensation for victims of crime. We have seen this evolution beginning with such statutes as the Ontario statute providing compensation for victims of crime and the formation in the Province of Ontario of the Criminal Injuries Compensation Board. At the beginning it was viewed as a remarkable departure, but now it has become more and more accepted and the concept of compensating victims of crime has been happily and speedily reconciled with other areas of tort law in criminal procedure.
I share the concern raised by the Hon. Member for Burnaby as far as factors in our society which lead to crime are concerned, and particularly reflect upon his point about violence on television. But a few weeks ago in my constituency of Etobicoke-Lakeshore we held a public forum on family violence. In the course of that evening's session, Ms. Diane Pone, who is with the National Clearing House on Family Violence of the federal Government, reported on a conference which she had just that week attended in Chicago.
Something which is now developing in the United States- and we in Etobicoke-Lakeshore are in the course of pursuing it-is to have people monitoring television programs on which there is undue violence, noting which companies are sponsoring those programs, communicating with those advertisers and asking them whether they realize the amount of violence being portrayed in the programs which they are sponsoring. If they do, they are asked whether they are consciously doing it or whether they would agree either to cease supporting the programs through their advertising dollars or at least give the program producers a reflection of the concern which they get from the community. I do not think that these questions can be solved once and for all, and in the abstract. 1 look on this as an important development at the local level. It is beginning to put public pressure reflecting the genuine community concern on those who are disseminating such an unwarranted level of violence through society over the air waves.
I should like to make my final point. Again reflecting upon my point about the local initiative to respond to some of the problems of violence and referring to the organization, Victims of Violence, it is interesting and perhaps timely that just 24 hours ago in my constituency office in Etobicoke-Lakeshore I
Crime Victims Assistance Act
was meeting with Gordon Kearns and his wife, Lillian. They are certainly aware of the issues which we are now discussing because their daughter and their two grandchildren were murdered. They, along with others, were the founders of Victims of Violence National Link. Lillian Kearns, a constituent of mine, is Treasurer of this organization. They provided me with two brochures which are being distributed by the organization-one called "It Could Happen to You" and the other, a more descriptive pamphlet of the services which this very important community organization is providing.
I should point out that the organization is referred to in the police brochures of both the Metropolitan Toronto Police Force and the Peel Regional Police Force. There is an effective working relationship between Victims of Violence National and these two police forces. One idea which is central here is that violence does not discriminate. Men, women and children at all levels, in all walks of society, are victims of crime. The concept that it could happen to you is never more true than in this area.
The representatives of Victims of Violence came to see me for the same reason they have been seeing the Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell). They have had difficulty with the Department of National Revenue getting registration for charitable purposes, which of course would be a great boon in their efforts to raise funds to continue their very worth-while support services to families who are cruelly bereaved through murder, or victims of other crimes. This is something on which the Hon. Member for Ontario and I are working, to see whatever changes are required in their application or their letters patent, and to see that whatever needs to be done be done swiftly so that the very important support work of the organization can proceed with all possible support.
That is one way in which community groups are doing their best. They will also get a very strong signal from the Government, from this Parliament, when the Bill which has been brought before the House by the Hon. Member for Halifax West is referred to committee and there considered fully so that we can, in turn, have proper legislation going forward for those too often ignored in the criminal justice process, the victims themselves. The ones who are most often forgotten or are left in the shadow of the process involving all machinery of justice, police investigation, criminal trial and incarceration, are the victims themselves. From speaking with the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Beatty) I know that he is extremely mindful of the role and importance of seeing that victims are getting a fair share of attention and that their rights are respected. In our criminal justice system, while doing all that is necessary and appropriate for those who have perpetrated crimes, we must be mindful that the rights of victims must be upheld.
I applaud the Hon. Member for Halifax West for bringing the Bill before the House. I join with other Hon. Members who have urged that the subject matter of the Bill go to committee and there, I hope, receive full and prompt attention.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege, and it gives me great pleasure to speak on this subject today.
In 1981 a young girl lost her life. A young man was allowed out on mandatory supervision. Her father came to me and asked me what he should do. We spent a great deal of time together over the next few months trying to find out if the local police department had been notified that the young man who had committed the crime had been released from prison. Unfortunately, due to a strike in an office somewhere between Kingston and Oshawa, the local police department was not notified of this.
The victim's father, Don Sullivan, was a very distraught man at that time. Don has had the courage, dedication and leadership to help bring this Bill to the House for second reading. Don has done a great deal for humanity and a great deal for Canadians. He had to suffer throughout the terrible period of the trial when he could not receive information and did not know if the young man who had killed his daughter was in or out of jail. He received absolutely no co-operation from enforcement officers.
Don Sullivan created Victims of Violence as a result of a phone call he received one night from a mother who had experienced the same kind of tragedy. The two of them started it all at a kitchen table in Scarborough.
In 1982, Don Sullivan came to me for help. He never asked for a hand-out. He never wanted a grant to help him try to represent the victims. Once he started doing this, many people began coming to him. He had long-distance telephone call expenses. He had lost his job as a taxi driver. He was unemployed for a short period of time and then took on a job with the Harbour Commission police force in Toronto.
In coming to me for help, Don only asked that his organization be permitted to try to raise money through donations that could be tax deductible. He wanted to get a tax number from Ottawa. I ran into roadblocks that I could not have imagined when trying to provide this man with a tax number to permit him to raise funds to pay for his long-distance telephone calls, his postage and the information he was sending to other suffering people across the country.
I would like to tell the House of one other thing that occurred in order to prove the importance of victims rights. The husband of a lady who lives about three miles from me. One night tried to stop a vehicle one night. The occupants were stealing some tires that were chained to a tree in a rural area. The vehicle with the people who were trying to steal the tires drove off, dragged the man down the road and killed him. To this day no one knows who was in that vehicle. The wife of the man who was killed has suffered through hell since that time. She was never kept informed of what the police were trying to do to resolve the crime. She was never told anything. She was kept in the dark.
Finally, I went to see Don and told him that I had a problem. I asked if he could help me. Don called this lady and went to see her. That is the kind of person he is. He did this
totally voluntarily. After he had seen her, she called me to tell me that she now felt she had someone with whom she could communicate. She realized that there was a group of people who had suffered the way she had.
Victims of crimes are ill treated and kept in the dark. We give all the protections that exist under the Bill of Rights to the murderers, the robbers and those who do wrong. However, we fail to look after those important members of our society who suffer, the victims. I suppose even I do not know how tough it is to experience a loss such as that suffered by Don Sullivan. However, I lived with his experience for some time.
Don has proved to be quite a force across the country. He has spent his own money. Organizations like Canadian Pacific Airlines have assisted him as he has travelled across the country. However, the only people who have not listened to Don Sullivan are those in the Government of Canada. 1 say hurrah to the Conservative Government. I am not being partisan, I am simply being supportive of Don Sullivan. The Conservative Government has taken this Bill seriously and is moving it to the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs so that we, on behalf of those people who have suffered, can deal with the issue of bringing into force victims' rights, and do for those people that which is absolutely essential in this day and age.
I must say that the former Solicitor General, the Hon. Member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), acted exceptionally. He visited Mr. Sullivan, listened to him and told him that he had to do something about this. Then he started doing something. I understand that the Department has been in touch with Don since then. However, the critical action is in the form of this Bill, and I would like to pay my sincere and heartfelt thanks to the Hon. Member for Halifax West for bringing it before the House. I myself have been trying to draft a similar Bill. I am not a lawyer, but along with my assistant we have been working on it in an attempt to make its provisions very thorough. Perhaps she will be able to have some input and offer information that will be required for the deliberations of the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
I also commend the Hon. Member for Burnaby who has been very active and supportive of victims over the years. As well, I would like to make particular mention of the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) who was very helpful in supporting me in the creation of the western arm of Victims of Violence. The Hon. Member was able to go with Don Sullivan to help the organization establish a branch in western Canada.
A great many people have been touched by Victims of Violence. A great many people have become more complete human beings through their understanding of the message Victims of Violence is trying to get across. I hope the next time I rise to discuss this Bill in the House, it will have been finalized and will be acceptable to all the victims who have suffered over the last many years.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIME VICTIMS ASSISTANCE ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to address the House this evening on the
January 23, 1986

subject of Bill C-241, the proposed Crime Victims Assistance Act. I too would like to extend my congratulations to the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) for bringing this very important subject before Parliament.
Victims of crime have a number of concerns relating to their role in the criminal justice system and the assistance they would like to have in order to participate in this system more fully and with greater awareness of their rights. In some cases, crime victims would like to see changes to the law that would enhance their status in criminal proceedings. This, of course, would have to be balanced with a number of factors, including the right of the accused to have a fair trial.
I have already received a letter from a lawyer in my riding of Niagara Falls who pointed out very thoroughly some of the problems an accused may have in getting a fair trial. However, at the same time, he and all of us recognize the need for more adequate protection of victims of crime. Any changes to the law must therefore give careful consideration to the many interests involved in order to ensure that the best solution is found to meet the concern in question.
The Bill before us attempts to ensure that adequate and fair compensation be awarded to crime victims.
Today, in Canada, crime victims have several means of recourse to some sort of compensation. First, there is the Criminal Code which makes limited provision for compensation, and the emphasis should be placed on the word "limited". I know that in most cases the victims of crime are not even aware of their right to appear before a court to make a claim for restitution.
Second, for many centuries the victims of crime have been able to pursue civil remedies, seeking redress through civil proceedings. Again, the utility of that measure is often called into question. Many times the perpetrator of the crime is an individual with no means of support. Other times the victim of the crime does not have the money to obtain legal counsel in order to pursue the matter through the courts.
There is also a third way by which victims of crimes can be compensated. I am referring to the criminal injuries compensation boards. I believe that in nine of the ten provinces, with the exception of Prince Edward Island, there is a criminal injuries compensation board in place. My experience in the Province of Ontario has not been very good in this respect. It is my belief that the awards by the Criminal Injuries Compensation Board of Ontario are not even coming close to compensating victims. Much more money, both from the federal Government and the provincial Government, has to go into this area.
Therefore, I believe there are shortcomings with respect to all three of the alternatives I have just mentioned. It is essential that the question of compensation be addressed in a much broader context, one that takes into account the existing measures to see how they can be improved upon.
Bill C-241 proposes to ensure that crime victims have access to compensation through criminal proceedings. It contemplates
Adjournment Debate
measures which go far beyond the present provisions, in some instances perhaps raising constitutional concerns. However, the spirit of the Bill is highly commendable. It attempts to provide for a one-stop shopping, more economical type of solution, providing for an enhanced role for victims in criminal proceedings, giving victims special standing in court proceedings and access to information which is not even available to the accused. These proposed changes, however, may not be the most desirable solution to address the issue of compensation to victims and the status of victims.
The question of how to provide assistance to crime victims has been under consideration in Canada at both levels of | Government. Both levels of Government have been actively following up on the 1983 task force report on justice for victims of crime. That report recommends a number of improvements, including legislative amendments which would better meet the concerns of victims. Compensation is one of the issues which received attention in the report. However, I do not think any solution in this area should be considered without reviewing, not just the task force report but all the different issues raised. That is why I believe there is a disposition in the House to have this matter referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for full consideration. Accordingly, I move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"Bill C-241, an Act to provide assistance for victims of crime, be not now
read a second time but that the Order be discharged, the Bill withdrawn and
the subject-matter thereof referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and
Legal Affairs."

subtopic: CHILDREN-CONVENING OF CONFERENCE ON MISSING CHILDREN
CHILDREN-CONVENING OF CONFERENCE ON MISSING CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my purpose in rising this evening to deal with the question I raised with the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) on December 18,

January 23, 1986
Adjournment Debate
1985, concerning missing children. I cannot help but think, as we have seen the disposition of the House with respect to the crime victims legislation which will now be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, that the House might have taken the same action with respect to a Bill I presented to the House on October 1, 1985, entitled the Missing Children's Search Act. Just as we considered crime victims in Private Members' Hour today, we might also turn our thoughts to the subject of missing children because, in many cases, those missing children are the victims of crime and criminal acts.
My specific reason for asking the Solicitor General that question on December 18, 1985, was that at of a press conference he held the day before in which he announced specific measures with respect to missing children. Among the measures announced by the Solicitor General was one to establish a central registry on missing children to be operated by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It would obtain and maintain facts and other information concerning missing children across Canada. In addition, the Solicitor General announced an intention to form a Canadian information centre on missing children. Beyond that, the Solicitor General promised a national missing children's day, presumably to focus attention on the subject of missing children across Canada. He said that there would be a national conference on missing children.
When asked in the House with respect to the matter he indicated that the conference would be held as soon as possible. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General (Mr. Towers) will give us some information on when that conference might be held.
In addition, the Solicitor General announced a missing children's research project for the City of Montreal, the purpose of which would be to examine the facts and circumstances related to missing children in that city with a view to making recommendations on what further action might be taken.
My first duty is to compliment and congratulate the Solicitor General on taking these steps, because the subject of missing children-and it is a broad subject-has been almost totally neglected at the national level for the past decades as the problem has developed on the streets of urban centres and the roads of rural centres across Canada. I do not apologize at all for raising this subject as many times as I am given the opportunity to raise it in the House of Commons because the subject of missing children is only the tip of a much deeper iceberg, that is, the social wrongs which prevail against children in our society.
The Solicitor General, as I said, has proposed a project for the City of Montreal. I would like to refer specifically to activities in that city. I have before me a newspaper clipping from December of 1985 which quotes Thom Garfat, who is the Director of Treatment at the Youth Horizons Reception Centre in Montreal. He points out very graphically what is at the heart of my concern.
First, the article indicates that over 120,000, and as many as 150,000, children ran away from homes in Canada in the year 1984. That makes it a major problem in terms of numbers. One has to ask oneself: What happens to these runaways who do not return home or are not returned home? Unfortunately, Mr. Garfat provides the answer:
After a short time, some turn to prostitution to support themselves. Or they end up involved in breaking and entering, stealing credit cards and cash. They may even like it.
That is the problem I want to address. I hope the Solicitor General (Mr. Crosbie) will give grave consideration to this problem in the days, weeks and months which lie ahead, because missing children either are or become the victims of criminal activity and that is what makes it a problem for law enforcement agencies across Canada.
The Government of Canada and the Governments of each and every province and territory would be derelict in their duties to the youth of Canada if they did not address in very specific terms what has become the problem called "missing children". I should say that not only runaways create the problem. An even greater problem lies in the fact that children are being taken from their home environment by strangers or, indeed, by members of the families in situations where there are custodial or other family disputes. The point is that across North America we have a large number of young people who have become known as "missing". But the real situation, as pointed out by Mr. Garfat, is that the missing children have become victims of crime or get themselves into a criminal situation. If clear steps are not taken to rectify this situation, death and other forms of violence will result.
In my city of Halifax we have had a graphic demonstration of the dangers to young people on the streets of cities. There have been three teenage murders in a very short period of time. In at least two of the cases, the young girls had been engaged in prostitution. I suppose there are some people who would say that that situation should deprive those victims of sympathy, but that is not so. Quite to the contrary, it is people in that situation who should attract our attention and our sympathy because a young teenage girl involved in prostitution is a victim of our social structure and is not, in most cases, a voluntary actor in that kind of involvement.
I want to present to this House as many times as 1 have the opportunity the subject of missing children. As it states in the headline I have before me, missing children have become a U.S. national preoccupation. There are television programs put before a national audience about this subject. I believe Canadians are responding to the challenge to do something about missing children. I hope the Solicitor General and the Government of Canada can play a real and important role in that challenge to resolve the problem of missing children.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: CHILDREN-CONVENING OF CONFERENCE ON MISSING CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a question to the Minister, the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) underlined the importance of measures we are taking on missing
January 23, 1986

children in Canada. He noted especially the urgent need for a national conference on missing children. I congratulate him on his initiative in bringing attention to this important matter.
While the main responsibility for the prevention, investigation and detection of missing children is on a local and provincial level, I feel there are a number of important steps which can be taken by the federal Government to respond to the problem. The most immediate and direct action which can be taken is to have the RCMP create a central registry of missing children in Ottawa in order to assist police forces and concerned agencies across Canada in locating and identifying missing children. An important by-product of such a registry is the generation of national statistics on missing children in Canada, data which we do not now have. We are also setting up four major research projects to examine the phenomenon of missing children in great detail. We must know much more about the dimensions of the problem and how different police departments attack the issue.
The first such project in Montreal should be up and going in about three months, thanks to the co-operation of the Quebec and Montreal urban community Governments. We are now negotiating with other jurisdictions with a view to developing three more research projects to delve into this complex problem. There will have to be continuing consultation between all levels of Government and provincial and municipal police forces, the private sector and, of course, the voluntary sector which has been doing so much good work in this area.
I see our role as one of getting the ball rolling and bringing the concerned parties together to collaborate and provide expertise from their own spheres of responsibility. To this end the Minister will convene in Ottawa in late April a national conference on missing children. This conference is urgently needed, as my hon. friend from Halifax West has noted. At this conference the Solicitor General will bring participants up-to-date on the development of the central registry and research projects. The conference will provide an important forum for the exchange of ideas and information. There will be a discussion on further measures that can be taken to respond to the problem of missing children.
Two important agenda items will be proposals made by the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) to establish the designation of May 25 as National Missing Children's Day to focus public attention on the measures that can be taken to minimize the risk of children becoming victims. The second item is for a Canadian Information Centre on missing children. The role and ambit of this Centre needs to be the subject of consultations with other levels of Government and the voluntary sector. However, I see it having the potential for an important role as a clearing house for the exchange of information on effective prevention programs and facilitating the co-ordination of efforts across Canada. It is our hope that private sector groups already involved with missing children will play an important role in the Centre.
Adjournment Debate
I must close, but in doing so let me say that I believe all Hon. Members and the people they represent are concerned for the thousands of children who go missing every year in Canada. They want to see elected representatives at all levels working with police and others to find solutions to this problem which causes so much needless anguish and suffering. I thank the Hon. Member for allowing us the opportunity of discussing this important matter at this time.

Mr. Speaker, on January 16 I applauded the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) for his swift action in announcing a major overhaul of the Young Offenders Act. That Act came into being in 1982, and Phase II came into effect as of April 1, 1985. It involved raising the minimum age at which a youth could be tried in an adult court from 16 to 18, as well as raising the age at which a youth could be prosecuted from seven to 12. I have spoken on this important and vital issue on at least five occasions over the past year. I have from the start been totally supportive of the basic principles and philosophy of the Young Offenders Act. 1 would like to now just highlight the four principles which underlie this important piece of legislation.
First, young people are personally responsible for their acts and should be held accountable before the law. Second, young people, like all Canadian citizens, enjoy rights which are protected by the Bill of Rights and Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Third, society has a right to be protected from criminal behaviour. Fourth and last, juvenile justice laws and procedures must recognize and deal with the fact that young people have special needs because they are at various stages of development and maturity. If there is any group in society that deserves that second or third chance, it is our youth.
The Solicitor General has promised a reform package of legislation within the next two months. I would just like to highlight what I believe will be forthcoming. These are major improvements.
First, the procedures and language of the Act sometimes makes it difficult for the authorities to deal quickly and effectively with young offenders who have, for example, violated probation conditions or failed to keep the peace. Such limits are clearly unacceptable. Second, the rules which govern detention after arrest are inflexible and can cause hardship for both police and the young people affected.
For instance, just today, Mr. Speaker, I was talking with Inspector Jim Clarke, head of the Youth Bureau for Metropolitan Toronto. He was highlighting again the problem of detention. Under current provisions, if two youths are apprehended and one is under 12 and the other over 12, they cannot be placed in the same cruiser to be taken home. We had an example of that where the youths were brothers, and yet could not be sent home in the same cruiser. Of course this

January 23, 1986
Adjournment Debate
causes, particularly small municipalities, a real problem in terms of cost.
Third, there appears to be circumstances in which the inability of police to make names or other identifying information publicly known has been an impediment to effective law enforcement or has created an unreasonable risk to the public. This concerns the problem of missing children which, by coincidence, was debated just a few minutes ago. While it is essentially a provincial matter, I believe the federal Government can show leadership to try to get more consistency in these age ranges that exist throughout the country. For instance, in Quebec I believe the limit is up to 17 and in Ontario it is 16. I think we could play a leadership role in that particular area.
Fourth, there were no comprehensive records systems under the old law, but the Young Offenders Act has introduced such systems clearly authorizing the use of fingerprints, youth court records in an adult court, and so on. Unfortunately, the records provisions have created a wide range of technical and administrative problems. Indeed, I am told that there was not even a clear definition of what constituted a record.
Fifth, Mr. Speaker, modifications should be made to the Criminal Code provisions dealing with counselling criminal behaviour. No one who abuses children by involving them in criminal acts should be immune from criminal prosecution.
Sixth, the current provision requiring that the evidence of a child witness be corroborated by other evidence is clearly unacceptable. The court should assess the testimony on its own merits. Similarly, an oral statement made by an accused who refuses to sign a written waiver should be admissible on its merit.
Seventh, the language of the Act is now unclear about the maximum length of sentence that may be applied for subsequent convictions. The courts should be capable of imposing appropriate sentences for new crimes, with the result that the total sentence for different offences could be longer than three years. The current maximum sentence under the Young Offenders Act is three years unless the case is referred to an adult court. Last April 12 a most regrettable crime was committed by a 14-year old in Scarborough, Ontario. Three people were murdered, yet the sentence given was only three years as provided by the Young Offenders Act. Fortunately, a family court judge has been asked to reopen the trial to determine if the case should be referred to an adult court.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, it appears that most of the major flaws in the Young Offenders Act will be corrected within a few months. The Solicitor General is to be commended for moving so sensitively and quickly to provide remedial action. He has listened to various concerned groups in society and acted wisely and compassionately. I commend and applaud him for that.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member for his interest in this very important matter of concern to all of us. I firmly support the basic principles and
philosophy of the Young Offenders Act. My belief in these principles has been confirmed in the discussions of the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) across Canada with concerned citizens, police, correctional workers, the legal profession, provincial authorities, and others. Not only did we need to reform the old juvenile justice system, but we needed a law to ensure that young people have the same rights and obligations as do adults.
The basic philosophy of the Young Offenders Act is as follows. One, young people are personally responsible for their acts and should be held accountable before the law. Two, young people, like all Canadian citizens, enjoy the rights that are protected by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Three, society has a right to be protected from crime. Four, juvenile justice laws and procedures must recognize and deal with the fact that young people have special needs because they are at various stages of development and maturity.
Certain provisions of the present law pose problems and it is up to the Solicitor General to deal with these problems, with all our support. Concerns about the handling of youth court records, the ban on publication of offenders' names and the difficulty of enforcing sentences are some of the major concerns which moved the Minister to initiate consultations across the country. He wanted to hear from those who work with the Act every day-judges, police, concerned citizens, youth court workers, Crown and defence counsel-to identify the nature of these concerns and get a good idea of what improvements were required.
The Government recognizes that the provinces and territories must be consulted on such important national matters. Parliament legislates criminal law but it is the provinces which must administer it. That means they have to do their part. In two areas in particular-providing the court with alternatives to sentencing a young offender to prison and providing adequate legislation to deal with children under the age of 12- the provinces have an especially heavy responsibility.
The deputy minister has been meeting with his provincial and territorial counterparts this week and the Solicitor General will be meeting with provincial and territorial colleagues early next month for a final discussion of proposed improvements. As soon as possible thereafter he will present to Parliament a package of amendments that will make the Young Offenders Act much more responsive to the concerns of those who have to work with it. He will be asking for the opposition parties' co-operation in passing the Bill as soon as possible.
Action is required to enable authorities to deal effectively and quickly with young offenders who have, for example, violated probation conditions and other conditions of their sentences. It is required to give police more flexibility in detaining young offenders after their arrest. The present rules at times cause hardship for the police and young offenders. It is required to allow publication of names in those circumstances where a young offender who might be a danger to the public has escaped custody or where public assistance is
January 23, 1986

needed to apprehend the offender quickly. Action is required to improve the Act's record-keeping provisions, which have caused a wide range of technical and administrative problems. These problems will be addressed and evident omissions resolved. The law will be clarified to ensure that records in cases of acquittal by reason of insanity are kept.
Action is required to ensure that modifications to the Criminal Code provision dealing with counsellig criminal behaviour are made to ensure that no one who abuses children by involving them in criminal acts will be immune to criminal prosecution. The Solicitor General will be discussing this point with our colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie).
Action is required to ensure that courts are capable of imposing appropriate sentences for new crimes with the result that the total sentence for different offences could be longer than three years.
I thank the Hon. Member for providing the opportunity of discussing this major issue at this time.

subtopic: VISIBLE MINORITIES-GOVERNMENT'S NEGOTIATIONS WITH REPRESENTATIVES OF JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II. (B) REQUEST FOR FURTHER NEGOTIATIONS
VISIBLE MINORITIES-GOVERNMENT'S NEGOTIATIONS WITH REPRESENTATIVES OF JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II. (B) REQUEST FOR FURTHER NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to review a question that I posed to the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Jelinek) on January 16. The date is significant because that is the date we learned of the U.S. Congress plans to move very boldly on three separate fronts with respect to the Japanese American citizens. One front was the personal compensation; the second was a foundation and the third was a general apology. I believe we should use the opportunity to compare what Canada is doing with respect to the Japanese Canadian redress issue.
I am sure my friend opposite will suggest that, looking to the past 43 years, the Government is making an attempt to correct a past injustice. However, the debate should take the perspective of what the Government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised when he was Leader of the Opposition. We should consider in perspective what the Prime Minister promised on the hustings during the last federal election when he said that the package needs to be negotiated and the wrongs need to be righted.
We should also consider this debate from the perspective of the Minister's predecessor who said in a press release dated December, 1985 that the Government would move on two fronts. First, it would negotiate a redress package and second, it would negotiate it with and through the National Association of Japanese Canadians which happens to be the legitimate body, elected across the country, to represent the views of the Japanese Canadian community. The Minister in his response said: "We are consulting, and I am consulting with the Japanese Canadian Association". I said during Question Period then, and I repeat it here tonight that that is a false and an untrue statement. I have met with membership organizations
Adjournment Debate
in Vancouver, in Winnipeg, in Toronto and in Ottawa. They all suggest the great and growing frustration which the community is having dealing with the Government, particularly with this new Minister. He is not consulting with this organization, Mr. Speaker. He is circumventing the organization. The national president of the association only had one opportunity to meet with this Minister and that was in the lobby of the Winnipeg airport for 20 minutes. Is that consulting, Mr. Speaker? Is that what you would call negotiating a redress package? Of course it is not.
The previous Minister stopped the negotiations after two meetings and tried unilaterally to propose a solution to Parliament. That failed miserably. There is movement afoot, words and rumour around Ottawa, that a second unilateral package may be forthcoming.
My question tried to get a commitment from the Government that this Minister would honour the statements, pronouncements and speeches made by his Prime Minister, that he would honour the commitment his predecessor, the former Minister of State for Multiculturalism, made in his accord last December stating the two proposals I outlined earlier.
That is what the Opposition is talking about. We are talking about the Government's promise and the Government's commitment to the Japanese Canadian community. Now we have a Minister who refuses even to meet with the national associations, let alone negotiate. We have also a Minister who is much more political and partisan in dealing with this issue than his predecessor. Not only is he playing up the differences that might exist in the community on a national issue-there are divisions on every national issue we debate, discuss and move in this House of Commons, but there is never unanimity-but after consulting you need to work with the national vehicles and this Minister is not doing so.
Another factor is that this Minister's advisory council on multiculturalism has taken a public stand against a negotiated compensation package. The advisory council is there to advise the Minister. Everyone knows that. In such a delicate and sensitive issue, in an issue the Government has yet to resolve, this Minister allows this council to publicly make the statement it did. The Japanese community, the Opposition Party and Canadians at large know perhaps why that public pronouncement was made, it seems this Minister is preparing the skid. It seems this Minister is asking this council to oil the skid. That is inappropriate. It is inappropriate because it does not give credibility to the commitment, the clear commitment the Government and the Prime Minister made with this Particular constituency.
In closing, I urge the Government to come clean on the matter. If the Minister rises repeatedly, as he does, and says "we are consulting with Canadians and, after we have consulted, we will arrange a package", that is fine. He is a Minister in charge of a national constituency; let him consult. What 1

January 23, 1986
Adjournment Debate
want to hear from the Government is that following the completion of his consultations with whomever he wants, whichever Canadian he chooses, he will return to the negotiating table, present his findings and, in a give and take atmosphere, negotiate a settlement that is not only appropriate and politically acceptable to the Minister or to the Government but also satisfactory to the concerns of the community which a redress package would attempt to address. It is only logical. Let us have the Minister live up to his Government's commitment. Have the consultations, but for goodness sake be honourable, be fair and be just. Return to the National Association and together strike an agreement of which the entire House and the country can be proud.

speakeroldname: Mr. Geoff Scott (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: VISIBLE MINORITIES-GOVERNMENT'S NEGOTIATIONS WITH REPRESENTATIVES OF JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II. (B) REQUEST FOR FURTHER NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) for raising this most important issue if only to set the record straight.
At the present time, the Minister of State for Multicultural-ism (Mr. Jelinek) is consulting broadly with Canadians on how we can show regret in a meaningful way for the past wrongs to Japanese Canadians. This matter is of concern to all Canadians as it relates to the subjects of equality and human rights.
Shortly after being appointed Minister of State for Mul-ticulturalism, the Hon. Member for Halton, called Mr. Art Miki, President of the National Association of Japanese Canadians, representing a major component of their community, to establish contact and organize follow-up meetings. The
Minister met with him and other representatives of the NAJC in Winnipeg on September 16, 1985, and again in Toronto on October 31, 1985.
These discussions focused on the following items: first, appropriate wording for a parliamentary resolution acknowledging mistreatment of Japanese Canadians; second, possible changes to the War Measures Act; third, a possible pardon for infractions of war-time regulations; fourth, possibility of restoring Canadian citizenship to those who were deported; and, fifth, a meaningful financial settlement.
The Minister has also met with other members of the Japanese Canadian community in several centres and has come to understand that there exists a wide range of views on the most appropriate solution to this issue. It is well known that the National Association of Japanese Canadians is having a study completed by Price Waterhouse and that they wish to have the results of the study before the Government acts.
I would share the views of the Hon. Member for York West, and I say that it is the hope of the Government that with the good will of all Canadians we will be able to arrive at a just and meaningful settlement to this issue.
[ Translation]
